name: Erythropoietin
lead: Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein hormone made mainly by the kidneys in response to low oxygen; it stimulates red blood cell production in the bone marrow. Its gene is switched on by hypoxia-inducible factors, and it signals through the EPO receptor and JAK2 [1][2][4][11]. Roughly 90 percent of adult EPO comes from fibroblast-like cells in the kidney cortex and about 10 percent from the liver [22].

Recombinant human EPO (epoetin alfa, approved by the US FDA in 1989 as Epogen) treats anaemia of chronic kidney disease and chemotherapy-related anaemia [11][22][33]. In sport and fitness communities it is known as an endurance-boosting performance drug, because raising red cell mass increases oxygen-carrying capacity. The appearance link runs through training: people who use it describe greater endurance and recovery capacity supporting more training volume, which in turn shapes physique, and some bodybuilding and endurance-sport circles discuss it alongside other performance drugs.

EPO became widely known to the public through cycling, from the 1998 Festina affair, in which police found EPO in a team car at the Tour de France [32], to the US Postal Service team case that the US Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) laid out in a 2012 reasoned decision [34]. Placebo-controlled research has found that EPO raises maximal laboratory performance in trained cyclists, while a 2017 trial reported no difference in submaximal tests or a mountain road race [36].

Beyond erythropoiesis, laboratory research has examined EPO as a neuroprotective agent, reporting that it crosses the blood-brain barrier in animals and reduces ischaemic brain injury [3][7][8]. Wikipedia describes broader EPO effects such as angiogenesis and neuroprotection as controversial, since human trials have not reproduced the benefits seen in animals [22]. US labels for epoetin products carry boxed warnings for increased risk of death, heart attack, stroke, venous thromboembolism and tumour recurrence in some patient groups [22].

paras: Therapeutic EPO, made by recombinant DNA technology, belongs to the erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs); examples named by Wikipedia include epoetin alfa (Epogen/Procrit), darbepoetin alfa (Aranesp) and epoetin beta. They are used for anaemia from chronic kidney disease, chemotherapy-induced anaemia, anaemia in inflammatory bowel disease and myelodysplasia.[22] Wikipedia lists epoetin alfa's approved uses as anaemia of chronic kidney disease, anaemia in people taking zidovudine for HIV, anaemia from myelosuppressive chemotherapy and reducing the need for donor red cell transfusions; it is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines, is prescription-only in the US, EU and Australia, and Amgen developed it.[33] A core curriculum review explains that a relative deficit of EPO is central to the anaemia of kidney disease, alongside iron deficiency.[23] A 1991 review anticipated that recombinant EPO would reduce or replace transfusions for some paediatric patients, particularly those with end-stage renal disease or anaemia of prematurity.[24] A 2025 systematic review examined recombinant EPO for refractory iron-deficiency anaemia in pregnancy.[25]

EPO is not a cosmetic drug. Its link to appearance is through physical capacity. Raising haemoglobin mass is described as the main lever for raising maximal oxygen uptake, because cardiac output and oxygen extraction are hard to change; more red cells carry more oxygen to working muscle, which can raise aerobic capacity and endurance.[26] People who use performance drugs in endurance sport, and some in physique sport, describe the aim as more training volume and faster recovery, which can support a leaner or more muscular build over time. Wikipedia's blood doping article notes that EPO's effect of raising haematocrit made it attractive to professional and amateur cyclists.[26] No study has tested EPO as a physique or looksmaxxing aid in healthy people.

EPO binds its receptor on erythroid progenitor cells, which lack their own kinase domain; binding triggers phosphorylation and activation of JAK2, driving survival, proliferation and maturation [4][11]. Wikipedia adds that downstream pathways include STAT5, PI3K and Ras/MAPK, that EPO acts mainly by promoting survival of progenitors through anti-apoptotic effects, and that mature red cells do not express the receptor.[22]

Production is regulated by oxygen: under hypoxia the transcription factor HIF-1 binds an enhancer of the EPO gene, and HIF-1 was found to be a general mediator of hypoxic transcription in many cell types [1][2][5]. HIF-2 alpha is described as the dominant isoform in kidney EPO production [11]. Baseline blood EPO is about 10 mU/mL and can rise up to roughly 1,000-fold under hypoxic stress.[22] Wikipedia gives its blood half-life as about five hours, and notes that Gregg Semenza, Peter Ratcliffe and William Kaelin received the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on how cells sense oxygen through HIF.[22]

Animal studies reported that systemically given recombinant EPO reduced focal ischaemic brain injury and that EPO receptors are present at brain capillaries [3][8]. Other work reported anti-apoptotic signalling involving Jak2 and NF-kappaB [10][7]. A 2002 paper reported that EPO therapy for acute stroke was safe and beneficial [9]. Wikipedia says that clinical trials in ischaemic tissues did not confirm the animal benefits.[22]

Wikipedia traces the idea of a hormone regulating red cell production to Paul Carnot, who with Clotilde-Camille Deflandre proposed a factor called hemopoietin around 1905-1906; later Eva Bonsdorff and Eeva Jalavisto coined the name erythropoietin, and Reissmann and Erslev showed that a blood-borne substance raises haematocrit. Goldwasser and Kung purified EPO in 1977, Lin and colleagues isolated the human gene in 1985, synthetic EPO was first used successfully to correct anaemia in 1987, and the FDA approved Epogen in 1989.[22] Biosimilar epoetins were approved in the European Union in 2007, with Retacrit and Silapo (epoetin zeta) approved in December of that year.[22][33]

Epoetin alfa became a large commercial product. Wikipedia reports that Medicare paid about US$2 billion for it in 2010, making it the single largest drug expenditure for that programme, and that a 2011 book by Kathleen Sharp, Blood Feud, alleged that Johnson & Johnson encouraged high-dose prescribing to boost sales; the article reports these as allegations, not established findings.[33]

Wikipedia says EPO has been banned in sport since the early 1990s but that no test was available until the 2000 Summer Olympics, with some athletes sanctioned earlier after confessing.[22] The Festina affair began on 8 July 1998 when customs officers stopped Festina soigneur Willy Voet at the French-Belgian border and found EPO, anabolic steroids and syringes; the team was expelled from the Tour on 15 July after its director admitted organised doping, and by December 2000 all nine Festina riders had confessed to EPO use.[32] In November 1998, eight of the nine Festina riders tested positive for synthetic EPO, and several had haematocrit values above the 50 percent limit.[32]

On 10 October 2012, USADA published a 200-page reasoned decision describing a doping programme at the US Postal Service team that it called the most sophisticated, professionalised and successful the sport had seen, with testimony from eleven former teammates; the decision named EPO, steroids and blood transfusions, and Lance Armstrong received a lifetime ban in August 2012.[34] Armstrong confessed to EPO and transfusion use in a January 2013 interview with Oprah Winfrey.[26][34]

Wikipedia also reports bans in mixed martial arts and tennis: UFC fighters Chael Sonnen and Ali Bagautinov tested positive for EPO in 2014, T.J. Dillashaw lost the bantamweight title and was suspended for two years in 2019, and Simona Halep's four-year ban was later reduced on appeal after a contaminated supplement was judged the likely cause.[22][26]

Wikipedia reports that recombinant EPO can be detected in blood because of small differences from natural EPO, such as post-translational modification, and that the first cycling test was used at the 2001 La Fleche Wallonne.[22] The athlete biological passport takes a different approach, tracking haemoglobin, haematocrit, red cell count and reticulocyte values against an athlete's own baseline and prompting targeted testing when values shift; the UCI began its blood module in 2008, and in its first three years 26 riders tested positive for EPO, 20 of them after an abnormal profile led to targeted testing.[35] Cobalt and HIF stabilisers that stimulate the body's own EPO have also appeared in cycling doping reports.[26]

Wikipedia reports that studies link EPO to higher maximal aerobic capacity and cites a 2017 study that found no difference from placebo at submaximal effort but better performance in EPO users at maximal effort.[22] That study, a double-blind placebo-controlled trial in The Lancet Haematology, randomised 48 healthy, well-trained male cyclists to eight weeks of epoetin beta or placebo. The EPO group had higher haemoglobin, maximal power output (about 352 versus 341 W) and VO2 max (about 60.1 versus 57.4 mL/min/kg), but submaximal power and race time on the Mont Ventoux climb did not differ, and adverse events were mild and similar between groups; the authors noted that participants were non-professional athletes.[36] Wikipedia also cites a 2007 study in which EPO raised VO2 max and improved submaximal endurance but a scaled effort reduced the endurance gain.[22]

Package inserts carry boxed warnings for increased risk of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboembolism and tumour recurrence, with risk rising when treatment drives haemoglobin above roughly 11 to 12 g/dL.[22] Epoetin alfa is described as generally well tolerated; common effects include high blood pressure, headache, joint pain and clotting at the injection site, and serious events such as allergic reactions, seizures and thrombotic events are rare. Chronic self-administration can raise haemoglobin and haematocrit to abnormally high levels, and in kidney disease targeting haemoglobin above 13.0 g/dL is associated with greater cardiovascular risk.[33]

The FDA issued a clinical alert in February 2007 and a Public Health Advisory on 9 March 2007 after the DAHANCA 10 trial of darbepoetin showed worse loco-regional cancer control, and a revised boxed warning limits use in cancer patients to chemotherapy anaemia.[33] Grokipedia likewise reports that medical use of recombinant EPO has been associated with increased mortality and serious cardiovascular events in some patient populations.[11] A phase 3 trial of the HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitor daprodustat in dialysis patients was framed by its authors around the possibly increased risk of stroke, myocardial infarction and other events linked to EPO and its derivatives.[27]

For sport, Wikipedia's blood doping article lists higher blood viscosity, polycythaemia, heart attack, stroke, pulmonary embolism and thrombosis among the health risks of raising red cell counts.[26] A 2020 sub-analysis of the cycling trial measured clotting markers: EPO raised resting P-selectin and E-selectin slightly, and after exercise E-selectin was about 15 percent and platelet factor 4 about 32 percent higher than in the placebo group; the authors noted that exercise itself shifts the blood toward clotting, that EPO may add to the risk, and that they measured biomarkers rather than clinical events.[37] Drug labels are the authoritative source for safety information.

Registered clinical trials of EPO products are largely in anaemia. They include phase 3 comparisons of biosimilar epoetin alfa with the reference product in chronic kidney disease and dialysis patients [12][15][16], long-term safety studies of a further epoetin [14][18], and trials of epoetin in leukemia and chemotherapy-related anaemia [17][19][20]. A phase 2 study begun in 1993 examined the time course of EPO activity in renal failure [21]. Comparative phase 3 trials have set newer agents such as roxadustat and luspatercept against epoetin alfa [27][28][29].

Neuroprotection has been tested in newborns: a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial enrolled 501 infants born at 36 weeks or later with moderate or severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, given EPO alongside therapeutic hypothermia,[30] and a separate randomised trial studied EPO for neuroprotection in preterm infants.[31] Wikipedia notes that early or late treatment of preterm infants is not recommended because retinopathy risk rises.[33] In healthy athletes, a placebo-controlled trial of EPO in well-trained cyclists examined laboratory and race performance [36] and clotting markers [37]. None of these tests EPO for appearance or looksmaxxing goals.

EPO is a prescription drug and its use for performance enhancement is prohibited in competitive sport.[22] It is best known to the public through cycling doping scandals, including the Festina affair and the US Postal Service programme.[22][32][34] Wikipedia also describes a 2019 Nobel Prize for the oxygen-sensing work that explains EPO regulation.[22] Newer drugs that raise EPO indirectly by stabilising HIF, such as daprodustat and roxadustat, are being compared with epoetin in kidney disease trials [27][28].

Altitude training, blood transfusion and other forms of blood doping aim at the same outcome of higher oxygen-carrying capacity; Wikipedia describes homologous and autologous transfusions, cobalt and HIF stabilisers alongside EPO.[26]

lore.intro: EPO is discussed in endurance and physique circles as the classic performance-enhancing hormone, and the public record of its use is largely from anti-doping cases and research trials rather than from forum threads.[22][32][34]

claims.believers: Athletes in the Festina and US Postal cases are described as using it on the premise that more red cells mean more oxygen and speed.[32][34]
claims.experts: A placebo-controlled trial found higher maximal laboratory power but no difference in submaximal tests or a mountain race in non-professional trained cyclists.[36]

claims.claim: EPO supports more training volume and recovery, which shapes physique
claims.believers: Users in endurance and physique sport describe greater capacity to train as the payoff.[26]
claims.experts: No study has tested EPO for body composition or appearance in healthy people.[26]

claims.believers: Before 2000 no test existed and athletes were sanctioned mainly after confessions or raids.[22][32]
claims.experts: Direct tests and the athlete biological passport now exist, and the UCI reported 26 EPO positives in the passport's first three years.[22][35]

claims.claim: EPO is a safe medically proven drug
claims.believers: Its approved status in kidney disease and chemotherapy anaemia is cited as proof of safety.[33]
claims.experts: Labels carry boxed warnings for death, heart attack, stroke, clots and tumour recurrence in some patient groups, and a 2020 analysis in cyclists found higher clotting-marker levels after exercise.[22][37]

claims.believers: Early animal and stroke papers reported neuroprotection.[3][9]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says human trials have not reproduced animal benefits, and newborn trials have tested EPO alongside cooling.[22][30]

claims.claim: Higher red cell mass always means better performance
claims.believers: Doping accounts treat haematocrit as the key number.[32]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that raised red cell counts increase blood viscosity and thrombosis risk.[26]

card.summary: A kidney hormone and anaemia drug used for endurance doping; indirect link to appearance, with serious cardiovascular warnings.
card.note: Prescription drug banned in sport; linked to cardiovascular events in some patient groups.

quick.overview:
Erythropoietin is the hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells. Injectable versions treat anaemia in kidney disease and chemotherapy patients.
It is known mostly as an endurance-sport doping agent. Clinical trials have been in anaemic patients, and none aimed at appearance.
quick.mechanism: It binds the EPO receptor on red-cell precursors, activating JAK2 signalling to increase red blood cell production. The body releases it more when oxygen is low.
quick.risks: It is an Rx-only drug. Reported risks in patients include cardiovascular events and increased mortality in some groups; it is banned in competitive sport.
